newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - US media spending growth to slow next year.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - US media spending growth to slow next year.

text.p: Spending by advertisers in major media will continue rising next year but at a slower rate than the strong gains in 1996, media buying experts said this week.

Media spending will climb 5.6 percent to $182.9 billion in 1997 in the United States, predicted Robert Coen, director of forecasting at the McCann-Erickson ad agency. That compares with the 7.6 percent rise expected for this year.
John Perrits, chairman of Zenith Media Worldwide, also forecast a slowdown in media spending, with North America's increase at 1.7 percent next year, compared with 2.5 percent this year.
He saw it as a broad retrenchment from a worldwide media spending boom in the last three years.
"We are going to see a little slower growth because we have probably had our peak year in this cycle," he said.

Media spending has climbed for the third year straight in 1996 on the back of growing economies in most countries, with activity buoyed in the United States by the presidential election and Olympic ad promotions.
Coen said the main factor slowing growth in 1997 is the loss of big advertising events -- the elections and the Olympics -- that accounted for more than $1 billion in ad spending.
But he said the expansion in media spending will continue, owing to a healthy economy and large marketing outlays.
"Consumers are employed now and confident about their jobs," he said, citing 10 million new jobs since 1992, when the ad business was fighting the end of the last recession.
Media experts see ad spending linked to the consumer economy more than to corporate profitability.
Coen disagreed with Zenith's Perrits about the likelihood that the expansion has begun to see its limits, saying that "this recovery has some time to go."
"We've had three years of good growth and there's a lot of concern that that's it," said Coen. "I don't think it is. I don't think the current recovery is going to end in three years."
Coen cited statistics showing that the last expansion in media spending lasted for 12 years, from 1975 to 1987.
Zenith's Perrits agreed that the expansion would continue until 1999, but he said future gains were likely to be less significant than those of the past few years.
In the global market, Perrits saw European media continuing to expand but he expected austerity ahead of the planned single European currency to start cutting into growth.
The Asia Pacific region, too, was seen gaining in the year ahead, helped by a recovery in the Japanese consumer market and growth in China and other developing nations.
For ad agencies, too, the boom is expected to moderate in 1997, agency chiefs said at the PaineWebber Media Conference, which ran through Friday.
The past two years have marked a time of "exceptional above-trend performance," said Fred Meyer, chief financial officer of Omnicom Group Inc., parent of the BBDO and DDB Needham agencies.

Meyer said double-digit growth will continue at Omnicom's foreign operations but "gradual moderation in the domestic market's growth" will temper overall performance. So far this year, revenue at Omnicom has climbed 18 percent, while profit per share is up 22 percent.

Omnicom's rival, Interpublic Group of Cos. Inc., which owns McCann-Erickson, has enjoyed robust growth too. Chairman Philip Geier concurred with estimates that his company, the largest media advertising company in the world, will show a gain in per share earnings of about 14 percent.

British ad companies Cordiant Plc, owner of Saatchi & Saatchi and Bates Worldwide, and WPP Plc, which owns Ogilvy & Mather, trail the American companies in financial performance, mainly because of costly acquisitions in the past decade.
But officials of both companies said their financial houses are in order and they are expecting solid gains.
